guard: The same program on the walker and on the engine produces the same value, the same log, the same refusal, and the same journal entry for entry - the step keys AND their order. (COUNTING suite, not fail-fast: every cell prints, so an aim is graded by NAME rather than by whichever cell is earliest.)

mutations.name: a binary expression evaluates its right operand first, so two effects journal in the wrong order
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: two effects in one binary expression
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: two effects in one binary expression
mutations.note: The value is 2 whichever operand ran first, so nothing about the OUTPUT notices. What notices is the journal: a step key's occurrence is allocated where the effect is reached, so swapping the operands swaps two entries and a resumed run replays into the wrong one.

mutations.name: an argument list is evaluated right to left, so two effects journal in the wrong order
mutations.find:
.map((a) => (a.type === "SpreadElement" ? `...${this.seam("iter", this.expr(a.argument as AnyNode))}` : this.expr(a)))
      .join(", ");
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: two effects in one argument list
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: two effects in one argument list
mutations.note: An argument list has no emitter choice about ORDER - JavaScript evaluates the emitted expression left to right - so the mutation that breaks it is one that reorders the emission. A first attempt reversed the map and reversed it back, which restores every position AND every emitted string: it survived, correctly, because it changed nothing.

mutations.name: a member read is emitted as a native index, so the host prototype is reachable on the engine
mutations.find: return done(this.seam("get", `${obj}, ${this.memberKey(node)}`), g);
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: refusals: a prototype member of a string
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: refusals: a prototype member of a string
mutations.note: A record has NO prototype to reach - `o.constructor` is undefined on both arms - so the cell that catches this is a string's, whose curated table refuses the name L4020. A native index answers the host String constructor there, which is a live capability inside a program that is supposed to have none.

mutations.name: a member WRITE is emitted as a native index, so the write path's own refusals stop happening
mutations.find: const write = (value: string): string => this.seam("set", `${obj}, ${key}, ${value}`);
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: refusals: a curated key on the write path
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: refusals: a curated key on the write path
mutations.note: The mirror of the read mutant above. A native write silently succeeds where the walker refuses: `__proto__` reaches the real prototype and a member onto a string is dropped on the floor. Measured before it was aimed: with the write native, these two corpus programs are the first to red, and the callable-then divergences below red with them.

mutations.name: a catch binds the raw thrown value, so a program reads a different error record
mutations.find: const caught = this.seam("caught", raw);
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: catching what a refusal throws
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: catching what a refusal throws
mutations.note: `__ctx.caught` rethrows the six classes no program may catch and otherwise hands the walker's frozen {code, kind, message}. `e.code` reads the same either way, which is why this survived until a program logged the WHOLE value: raw, the engine hands back {code, name} - a different record, and one carrying a host class name.

mutations.name: a spread iterates natively, so a record stops being refused
mutations.find: return el.type === "SpreadElement" ? `...${this.seam("iter", this.expr(el.argument as AnyNode))}` : this.expr(el);
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: refusals: not iterable
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: refusals: not iterable
mutations.note: L4015 says arrays and strings and nothing else. A native spread of a record throws a host TypeError instead, which is a different class the program cannot catch the same way.

mutations.name: an object literal's properties are emitted in reverse, so two effects journal backwards
mutations.find: return this.seam("born", `{ ${parts.join(", ")} }`);
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: two effects in one object literal
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: two effects in one object literal
mutations.note: A record's own key order is observable through `keys`, `entries` and `json.stringify`, and the order its property values were EVALUATED in is observable only in the journal. This moves both.

mutations.name: a template's interpolations are emitted in reverse, so two effects journal backwards
mutations.find: return this.seam("template", `[${quasis.join(", ")}], [${exprs.join(", ")}]`);
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: two effects in one template
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: two effects in one template
mutations.note: Interpolation is the seam's law, but WHICH value goes into which hole, and in what order the holes were evaluated, is the transform's.

mutations.name: an array literal's elements are emitted in reverse
mutations.find: return this.seam("born", `[${parts.join(", ")}]`);
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: two effects in one array literal
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: two effects in one array literal
mutations.note: The third of the three literal positions where two effects can sit side by side.

mutations.name: a corpus program refuses before it reaches its subject, and the gate calls it identical
mutations.find: ["curated methods", 'const xs = [3, 1, 2]; log(xs.map((x) => x + 1), sort(xs), "AB".toLowerCase(), "a,b".split(","), (2.6).toFixed(1), json.stringify({ a: 1 }));', {}],

mutations.cell: every corpus program completes, or refuses the code it declares

This is a fixture-discipline cell, so its mutant is in the fixture.

mutations.name: a scope body evaluated at the call, so its effects journal outside the scope

Evaluated at the call, the engine journals the sleep first - a journal the walker's run never wrote, which a resume would then replay against.

mutations.name: the options bag is deferred along with the body, so the key is computed inside the scope
mutations.find: return defers && i === 1 ? `async () => (${code})` : code;

mutations.cell: identical on both engines: a fan-out whose key is awaited

Wrapped in a thunk it is computed inside, and the two entries swap. The ruled position is the BODY alone, so this mutant keeps every eager-body program green and shows up only as journal order in the program whose key awaits.

mutations.name: a primitive is spelled in a corpus program the run never reaches, so a kind is covered on paper
mutations.expectRed: and a corpus program journals every kind the engine can write
mutations.cell: and a corpus program journals every kind the engine can write

The name is still SPELLED, so the free-name cell stays green and both arms still agree; only a kind the engine actually wrote to a journal counts here, and `monitor` stops being one. Measured before it was aimed: this is the only cell that reds.

mutations.name: the dead-zone rule never looks at writes, so an early write dies as a native ReferenceError
mutations.find:
this.deadZone(b);
  }
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: a dead-zone write, plainly
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: a dead-zone write, plainly

mutations.name: the survival list points at a corpus row that completes, so the check is a comment
mutations.find: ["issue 642 through the set door: a callable then, then any later reference to the record", "refusals: a callable then, then a later reference to the record"],
mutations.replace: ["issue 642 through the set door: a callable then, then any later reference to the record", "absence and NaN are data, and still log"],
mutations.expectRed: the oracle's own process survives it, and hands the refusal back to its caller: issue 642 through the set door
mutations.cell: the oracle's own process survives it, and hands the refusal back to its caller: issue 642 through the set door: a callable then, then any later reference to the record
mutations.note: Surviving is not the claim; coming back as the ruled refusal is. Point the entry at a corpus row that COMPLETES and the child prints COMPLETED with exit 0 - the lookup still finds a row, the process still survives, and a check reading only the exit code would stay green over a section that had stopped measuring the value law at all.

mutations.name: the survival list names a corpus row that is gone, so it checks a program the gate no longer runs
mutations.find: ["issue 642 through the set door: a callable then, then any later reference to the record", "refusals: a callable then, then a later reference to the record"],
mutations.replace: ["issue 642 through the set door: a callable then, then any later reference to the record", "refusals: a callable then written onto a rekord"],
mutations.expectRed: the survival check names a corpus row that still exists, so the two cannot drift apart: issue 642 through the set door
mutations.cell: the survival check names a corpus row that still exists, so the two cannot drift apart: issue 642 through the set door: a callable then, then any later reference to the record
mutations.note: This list held its programs as LITERALS until now - two copies of each source with nothing keeping them equal, on the one section whose job is to stop those rows hanging the suite, so a drift would have been silent and green. The programs live in the corpus and are looked up by name, which removes text drift entirely; what remains is a row that is renamed or deleted out from under the reference, and that is what this mutant is. Note what it does NOT grade, since the lookup only asks whether A row was found: pointing the entry at a DIFFERENT row that exists passes this cell, and is caught by the mutant above it only because that row completes.

mutations.name: the child swallows a failure that escaped the caller, so an uncatchable refusal reads as a caught one
mutations.expectRed: the oracle's own process survives it, and hands the refusal back to its caller: issue 642 through the set door
mutations.cell: the oracle's own process survives it, and hands the refusal back to its caller: issue 642 through the set door: a callable then, then any later reference to the record
mutations.note: The OTHER clause, and the one the whole section exists for. These three used to fail in ways a corpus row cannot report - one killed the interpreter's process outright, two never settled - so what the cell has to notice is a refusal that does NOT come back catchable. Break the child's catch and the failure escapes exactly as it used to: the process dies, nothing is printed, and the cell reds on the exit code. Without this mutant the survival clause is graded by nothing, because no program left in the language still kills the oracle.

mutations.name: `undefined` is emitted as the global name, so a module the gate runs is no longer closed
mutations.find: if (VALUE_NAMES.includes(name)) return VOID;
mutations.expectRed: every program the gate runs emits a module with no free identifier, which is what the compartment cannot catch
mutations.cell: every program the gate runs emits a module with no free identifier, which is what the compartment cannot catch
mutations.note: Measured: NOT ONE behavioural cell in this suite reds. The free name resolves to the real global in the harness's evaluator, and lane H measured that inside the shipped SES compartment an unbound READ answers `undefined` and throws nothing either - so both arms agree, every journal matches, and the only thing that notices is the resolver over the emitted text. That is the whole argument for running it over the corpus this gate actually executes.

mutations.name: the shape leg is never compared, so the gate is back to comparing renderings
mutations.find: if (shapes(a.logs) !== shapes(b.logs)) out.push("log shapes");
mutations.expectRed: the comparator finds a difference the rendering cannot show: absence against a literal null
mutations.cell: the comparator finds a difference the rendering cannot show: absence against a literal null
mutations.note: A comparator-discipline cell, so its mutant is in the comparator. Every corpus row still passes without this leg - that is the whole point, the blindness was latent - so only the hand-built pairs notice, which is what makes them the evidence that the leg can fail at all.

mutations.name: the shape signature goes shallow, so a record carrying a function reads as an empty one
mutations.find:
: typeof v === "object"
            ? carriesCode(v)
              ? "object+code"
              : "object"
            : typeof v;
mutations.expectRed: the comparator finds a difference the rendering cannot show: an empty record against one carrying a function
mutations.cell: the comparator finds a difference the rendering cannot show: an empty record against one carrying a function, which is the nesting a shallow signature missed
mutations.note: The first spelling of this signature WAS shallow, and lane H measured that it failed the two rows it had been added for: `{ g: (x) => x }` and `{}` both read `object`, and it is the NESTED closure rather than the bare one that killed the worker with a DataCloneError. The top-level pairs still pass shallow, so only the nesting controls red.

mutations.name: negative zero loses its sign in the signature, so `0 / -1` reads as zero
mutations.find:
: Object.is(v, -0)
      ? "-0"
mutations.expectRed: the comparator finds a difference the rendering cannot show: zero against negative zero
mutations.cell: the comparator finds a difference the rendering cannot show: zero against negative zero, which `0 / -1` produces in an ordinary program
mutations.note: Lane H's second hole in the first spelling. JSON draws -0 as `0` and so does a bare `typeof`, and `0 / -1`, `-0` and `0 * -1` are three ordinary programs that produce a true one, measured on both arms - they are corpus rows now, so this bit has live evidence and not only a control.

mutations.name: a cell is renamed and its aim is left behind, on this suite's config
mutations.find: ["a dead-zone write, plainly", "const f = () => { n = 1; }; f(); let n = 0; log(n);", {}, "L2004"],
mutations.replace: ["a dead-zone write, on its own", "const f = () => { n = 1; }; f(); let n = 0; log(n);", {}, "L2004"],
mutations.expectRed: every mutation's expectRed names exactly one cell this suite printed
mutations.cell: every mutation's expectRed names exactly one cell this suite printed
mutations.note: A corpus row's name IS a cell's name here, so renaming a row is how this suite's aims go stale - and it changes no behaviour, so no other cell reds. Aimed at the row this config already anchors on, which is the pair most likely to drift together in a future edit. The rename REPLACES the trailing word rather than extending it: expectRed is matched as a substring, so `..., plainly enough` still contains `..., plainly` and the stale aim keeps matching. Measured as a SURVIVOR in that spelling before this one.

mutations.name: both crossings are handed a record the replaying engine does not speak, so the comparison has nothing to compare
mutations.find: const back = { runId: "d", handler: new SimHandler({}), pins, onLog: (l: { values: readonly unknown[] }) => logs.push([...l.values]) };
mutations.replace: const back = { runId: "d", handler: new SimHandler({}), pins: { ...pins, languageVersion: "2" }, onLog: (l: { values: readonly unknown[] }) => logs.push([...l.values]) };
mutations.expectRed: and the two finished journals are the same journal, entry for entry, with two journals there to compare
mutations.cell: and the two finished journals are the same journal, entry for entry, with two journals there to compare
mutations.note: The control that found the false green, kept as the mutant that grades its guard. Both resumes refuse L5008, both finish cells red, and BEFORE the guard this comparison still printed ok with entries [0, 0] - two identical empty placeholders comparing as agreement. The fault cannot be manufactured any other way: a comparison of two subjects only lies about them when BOTH are absent, so the mutant has to kill both crossings. It is aimed at the comparison rather than at the finish cells it also reds, which this COUNTING suite grades by name.

mutations.name: the crossing is handed back to the engine that wrote the journal, so the refusal cell no longer crosses anything
mutations.find: const crossed = await resumeOn(other, source, original.journal, original.pins, across);
mutations.replace: const crossed = await resumeOn(wrote, source, original.journal, original.pins, across);
mutations.expectRed: and the engine refuses that journal by name, naming the version that wrote it and its own: sleep and the run clock
mutations.cell: and the engine refuses that journal by name, naming the version that wrote it and its own: sleep and the run clock
mutations.note: A refusal cell whose subject stops being a crossing is the circular-check class in its purest form: the record and the reader are the same engine, nothing disagrees, and the cell would report a refusal that never happened. Aimed at one program by name because every crossing prints its own cell.

mutations.name: the writer's own resume is sent to the other engine, so the replay half tests the refusal instead
mutations.find: const own = await resumeOn(wrote, source, original.journal, original.pins, again);
mutations.replace: const own = await resumeOn(other, source, original.journal, original.pins, again);
mutations.expectRed: the walker resumes the journal it wrote itself, reading it rather than dispatching: sleep and the run clock
mutations.cell: the walker resumes the journal it wrote itself, reading it rather than dispatching: sleep and the run clock
mutations.note: The mirror of the crossing mutant, and the reason both halves are asserted: with the replay half pointed across engines the suite would prove only that engines refuse each other, and would no longer prove that a journal can be resumed at all.

mutations.name: a resume that is handed pins re-resolves them instead of binding them, so a record's own pins are lost
mutations.find: ? bindPins(options.pins, options, ENGINE_LANGUAGE_VERSION)
mutations.expectRed: and when pins DO come with that empty journal the engine keeps them rather than resolving its own
mutations.cell: and when pins DO come with that empty journal the engine keeps them rather than resolving its own
mutations.note: The half of the empty-journal rule that CAN be graded narrowly. Re-resolving from the same options reproduces every default, so the cell carries one value no resolver would produce (a stepBudget of 12345) and this mutant is what proves that matters. The other half - an empty journal with no pins is a store, not a resume - is ungraded here by measurement rather than by oversight: its only mutant refuses every corpus run and kills the process (133 reds, no summary line), which grades a dead run instead of a cell.

mutations.name: the engine reports no steps, so the two engines stop being tellable apart by their unit
mutations.find: return { value, journal, programHash, pins, steps: engine.steps() };
mutations.replace: return { value, journal, programHash, pins, steps: 0 };
mutations.expectRed: the same program charges a different number of steps on each engine, so which one ran is observable at all
mutations.cell: the same program charges a different number of steps on each engine, so which one ran is observable at all
mutations.note: The control for every cell that watches WHICH engine ran something. If the engines stop differing observably, a dispatch cell keeps passing while observing nothing - it goes quiet rather than red - so the difference itself is asserted here and this mutant is what proves the assertion has teeth.

mutations.name: the engine stamps the walker's version into the record it writes, so the pin has nothing to disagree with
mutations.find: : resolvePins(options, options.handler.now(), ENGINE_LANGUAGE_VERSION);
mutations.expectRed: the record the engine writes is stamped with the engine's own language, which is what the other one later disagrees with
mutations.cell: the record the engine writes is stamped with the engine's own language, which is what the other one later disagrees with
mutations.note: The naive bump seen from the other end: with both engines stamping one version every crossing succeeds and the split refuses nothing. Written as a literal rather than as the walker's constant because host.ts does not import it, and a mutant that fails to COMPILE grades a dead run instead of a cell.

mutations.name: a matrix row cites a sentence this suite no longer prints, which is what a rename leaves behind
mutations.find: ["the walker resumes the journal it wrote itself, reading it rather than dispatching: sleep and the run clock"]
mutations.replace: ["the walker resumes the journal it wrote itself, reading it rather than dispatch: sleep and the run clock"]
mutations.expectRed: every row this suite owns is a sentence this suite printed
mutations.cell: every row this suite owns is a sentence this suite printed
mutations.note: The index's whole reason for being checked instead of written down. A citation is a copy of a sentence that lives somewhere else, and a copy drifts: here the row's text loses two characters, exactly the way a reworded cell leaves its index entry behind. Nothing else in the suite notices - the cell it names still runs and still passes under its new name - so this cell is the only thing between the matrix and a row list that describes a suite that has moved on.

mutations.name: a matrix row cites a sentence the runtime suite's list does not carry, and the cross-package half stops being checked
mutations.find: "and it is stamped with the version of the ENGINE that ran it, not with the current language",
mutations.replace: "and it is stamped with the version of the engine that ran it, not with the current language",
mutations.expectRed: the dispatcher rows and that suite's own list name the same sentences, each exactly once
mutations.cell: the dispatcher rows and that suite's own list name the same sentences, each exactly once
mutations.note: The same drift across the package line, where it is likelier and worse: the dispatcher rows are asserted in implementations/runtime, which cannot be reached from a lang suite except by reading its source, and a lang author has no reason to look there. One word loses its capitals and the citation resolves to nothing. If this cell did not exist, the matrix would keep claiming eight rows while three of them named sentences no suite anywhere prints.

mutations.name: a matrix row is dropped, and every surviving citation still resolves
mutations.find: ["3. a v2 record with entries, on the walker: refused L5008 — the defence behind the dispatch, for a caller who reaches past it", HERE, ["and the walker refuses that journal by name, naming the version that wrote it and its own: sleep and the run clock"]],
mutations.expectRed: the index carries all eight rows, in order, and none of them can be dropped quietly
mutations.cell: the index carries all eight rows, in order, and none of them can be dropped quietly
mutations.note: The failure the two citation cells are both blind to, because both quantify over the rows that are THERE: an empty matrix satisfies them perfectly. The row removed here is the one only this package can own - a v2 record forced onto the walker's own entry point - so its loss is the loss of the arm observation itself, and without the ordinals it costs nothing. This is why the labels carry numbers.

mutations.name: a row's citation is deleted, so the runtime suite lists a cell no row indexes
mutations.find:
"and the refusal says the record names none, rather than interpolating the missing value",
    ]],
mutations.expectRed: the dispatcher rows and that suite's own list name the same sentences, each exactly once
mutations.cell: the dispatcher rows and that suite's own list name the same sentences, each exactly once
mutations.note: THE DIRECTION THE OTHER SUITE'S OWN CELL CANNOT SEE, and the reason this half is set equality rather than containment. That suite asserts every sentence in its list executed; it cannot know whether any row here still cites them. Drop one citation and its cell stays green while the row it belonged to quietly indexes one fact fewer. Only the uncited direction catches it, and a matrix that silently loses a citation is the failure the whole index exists to prevent.

mutations.name: the seam file is written for another suite, and this matrix indexes it anyway
mutations.find: "suite": "implementations/runtime/smoke/run-driver.smoke.ts"
mutations.expectRed: the seam file this half trusts is the one the dispatcher's own suite writes
mutations.cell: the seam file this half trusts is the one the dispatcher's own suite writes
mutations.note: A seam is only a seam while both ends agree which subject it is about. This half now trusts a FILE rather than the other suite's source, so it must check the file is that suite's - otherwise a list written for any suite in the repo would satisfy the equality and the rows would index cells that never ran here. The runtime suite grades the same field from its own end; this grades it from the end that consumes it, which is the end that would be silently wrong.

mutations.name: the log sink hands the line over before it refuses, so the closure crosses and the refusal is cosmetic
mutations.expectRed: caught by the program, which then continues
mutations.cell: declared divergence, and both answers are what the ruling says: a log line is data on the engine: caught by the program, which then continues
mutations.note: WHY THAT ROW EXISTS, and it no longer reds alone - deliberately. The rule's value is the sink's POSITION, refused before the line reaches any transport. When this mutant was written the three uncaught rows could not see position at all, because `answer` collapsed a refusing arm to its code and threw its logs away: run it against them and all three were BYTE IDENTICAL while a live closure reached the host on every one. That measurement is what removed the collapse, so this now reds four cells and is graded on the caught row, whose subject IS the position seen from inside the program - the others see the emitted line, this one sees that the program caught, read the code, and continued past it.

mutations.name: a retired divergence is repaired by re-pinning both arms instead of being deleted
mutations.find: ["ruling 1c / issue 646: an update's operand is a numeric string", 'let n = "5"; n++; log(n);', {}, 'logs [[6]] shapes [["number"]]', "L4018 logs [] shapes []"],
mutations.replace: ["ruling 1c / issue 646: an update's operand is a numeric string", 'let n = 5; n++; log(n);', {}, 'logs [[6]] shapes [["number"]]', 'logs [[6]] shapes [["number"]]'],
mutations.expectRed: every declared divergence names two different answers
mutations.cell: every declared divergence names two different answers, so a retired one cannot be re-pinned into a permanent row
mutations.note: The failure this list is built to prevent, in the shape it actually arrives in. Issue 646 lands, the walker stops coercing, the row reds - and the repair that costs least is to re-pin BOTH sides to the new common answer, which leaves a program that agrees on both arms sitting inside the declared-divergence list, passing forever and counted as a divergence in the line printed above it. The mutant is exactly that repair: the row's own cell still passes by construction, and only the guard sees it.

mutations.name: a refusing arm's answer collapses to its code again, so a divergence that aborts compares nothing else
mutations.find: const answer = (a: Arm): string => `${a.error !== null ? `${a.error} ` : ""}logs ${j(a.logs)} shapes ${shapes(a.logs)}`;
mutations.replace: const answer = (a: Arm): string => (a.error !== null ? a.error : `logs ${j(a.logs)} shapes ${shapes(a.logs)}`);
mutations.expectRed: a log line is data on the engine: a function value
mutations.cell: declared divergence, and both answers are what the ruling says: a log line is data on the engine: a function value
mutations.note: The blind spot itself, restored. Five of the eight declared divergences end in a refusal on one arm, and with the collapse back in place each of them is pinned to a bare code that says the arm refused and nothing about what it had already done first - which is how a sink that hands its line to the host and refuses afterwards satisfied the pin exactly. This reds all five; it is graded on the first, and the note is here because a reader who sees five cells go red at once should know they are one fact, not five.

mutations.name: the sweep behind the entry leg's premise goes blind to one kind JSON flattens
mutations.find: if (Object.is(v, -0)) return [`${path} = -0`];
mutations.expectRed: finds everything a rendering flattens
mutations.cell: the sweep behind that premise finds everything a rendering flattens, nested where an entry would carry it
mutations.note: A zero is only worth the instrument that produced it, and this instrument's whole job is to see the values a rendering hides. Drop the negative-zero clause and the premise cell still reports its clean zero over 160 entries - unchanged, green, and now blind to `0 / -1`. Only the control that shows the sweep finding one of each kind can tell those two zeros apart, which is why the control exists and why it is graded here rather than the premise.

mutations.name: the entry sweep stops collecting, so its zero is a zero about nothing
mutations.find: scanned.push([`${name} / walker`, w.entries], [`${name} / engine`, e.entries]);
mutations.expectRed: and the sweep that says so visited every one
mutations.cell: no journal entry the corpus produces carries a value JSON cannot draw, and the sweep that says so visited every one
mutations.note: The other way a zero lies, and the reason the count and the finding are one cell over one array rather than two cells over two. With the collection gone the sweep has nothing to walk, reports no blind value, and would have passed as `blind.length === 0` alone - a green certifying a journal it never opened. Both halves read `scanned`, so this reds instead of going quiet.

mutations.name: the sweep walks a Date, a Map and a Set as if they were records, and finds them faithful

const proto = Object.getPrototypeOf(v) as object | null;

mutations.expectRed: finds everything a rendering flattens
mutations.cell: the sweep behind that premise finds everything a rendering flattens, nested where an entry would carry it
mutations.note: The clause a reader would delete first, because it looks defensive rather than load-bearing. Without it the walk recurses into a `Date`, a `Map` and a `Set`, finds no own enumerable key on any of the three, and reports all three faithful - while JSON draws the date as its own ISO string and both containers as `{}`, so a full Map and an empty record compare EQUAL in the entry leg. The control asserts an exact count rather than a non-zero one, which is what makes every clause of the sweep load-bearing; this one is spelled out because it is the one whose absence looks like nothing is missing.
